Hello there. You're looking at the newest version `of my text box sprite, version 2.5.
This text box has many different features, and `is pretty easy to use as well.
As you already know, you can set a name for `each line of dialogue to show who's speaking.
...that's basically the only similarity lol

One of the bigger features of this is that you can `change how the text moves within the text box.
Now, you're likely thinking, "Hey, this isn't new! `I saw you putting this to use in TM 1 and 2!"
And you're right. That's true. But the reason I'm `calling it new is because I've added more types `of motion.
Let's go through them, shall we?
Motion = 1 `Shaking Text `The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
Motion = 2 `Wavy Text `The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog~
Motion = 3 `Stuttery Text `The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog...
Motion = 4 `I Don't Even Know What This One Is `tHe QuIcK bRoWn FoX jUmPs OvEr ThE lAzY dOg!!!1
Motion = 5 `Emphasis! `The quick brown fox JUMPS over the lazy dog!
Motion = 6 `Shaking Text Box `The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog?!
And that's all of them. Cool, right?
But that's not all you can do with this sprite, `either.
You can also have a different sound play while the `dialogue is being typed out. Hear it?
This is useful for having a different noise for `every person speaking.
You can also change what the text box itself `looks like, as seen here.
For example, you can make the box look like a `piece of paper when someone is reading off one. `(I didn't make a graphic for that.)
Finally, you can make the text box wait for a `period of time before moving on to the next line of `dialogue.
This is done by entering "[[wait" as an item in `the dialogues list.

And now we move on to the differences between `this version and the previous version.
You may have noticed right off the bat that the `text box is smaller than it was before.
I made that change because with four lines of `space, it could get to be kind of obstructive.
The main difference, though, is how the non-`dialogue part of the sprite is formatted.
For example, the string shown above results in `what you see here.
Here's another example.
The first character determines what sound is `played while typing.
The second character determines how the text `moves.
The third character determines which costume `is used for the text box.
The rest of the string is then interpreted as `the name of the person speaking.
It sounds complicated, but it's really not that `bad if you know what you're doing.
And I guess that wraps up this showcase! `Feel free to use this sprite in your projects, but `please be sure to give me credit for it if you do.
